passages.original: Virgi- nis itaque si quis velit diligenter considerare vocabulum , ex virtutis inveniet nomine derivatum :virgo enim dicitur, quasi virago : viraginem vero Scriptura sancta non ob aliud vocatam dicit, nisi quia de viro sumpta est. Hoc autem a sancto Hieronymo secundum Hebraicam proprietatem libri Geueseos docet eipressa translatio, in qua sic habetur : Immisit ergo Dominus Deus soporem in Adam : cumque obdormisset, tulit unam de costis ejus, et replevit carnem pro ea, et ædificavit Dominus Deus costum quam tulerat de Adam in mulierem, et adduxit eam ad Adam ; dixitque Adam : Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de carne mea. Hæc vocabitur Virago, quonium de viro sumpta est (Genes.
passages.english: So if anyone is willing to consider carefully the word "virgin" (virgo), he will find it derived from the name of virtue (virtus): for virgo is said as if virago; and Holy Scripture says that the virago was so called for no other reason than that she was taken from man (vir). This is shown by the translation made by Saint Jerome according to the Hebrew idiom of the book of Genesis, in which it reads thus: "So the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place; and the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam; and Adam said: This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called Virago, because she was taken from man" (Gen.
passages.notes: The Latin wordplay virgo/virtus/virago/vir cannot be rendered in English; the Latin terms are kept in parentheses. Scanning errors corrected (Geueseos = Geneseos, eipressa = expressa, costum = costam, quonium = quoniam). The reference continues in the following context (2:21-22).

Cernis nempe quomodo beatus Augustinus nullam hic separabilium personarum suspicioriem relinquit, quando Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum sanctum, sic- ut inseparabiles sunt, sic 238 inseparabiliter asserit operari. Quam sententiam tali conclusione confirmans (Cap.
passages.english: III, 22), when the Son was baptized by John, and when the voice sounded, saying: "I have both glorified [it], and I will glorify [it] again" (John 12:28), yet, showing that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, he added this statement, saying: "Although the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, so work inseparably." You see, surely, how blessed Augustine here leaves no suspicion of separable persons, when he asserts that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, so work inseparably. Confirming this statement with the following conclusion (Chap.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference and mid-sentence; the main verb of the sentence begun in the preceding context is somewhat loose. The quoted clause of Augustine is concessive and incomplete as cited. The number 238 is a page marker and is omitted.

XVI, 27). utique ipse non aeparat; sed secundum ea fdcit intelligi, quæ supra commemoravi, satisque insinuavi, plerumque ita nominari unamquamque in Trinitate personam, ut et aliæ illic intelligantur. Sic itaque dictum est : Ipse enim Pater amat vos, ut consequenter intelligatur et Filius, et Spiritus sanctus. Item post aliquanta (Cap. 12, ante medium) idem sanctus Augustinus sic ait: Jam enim ostendimus in hac Trinitate per multos locutionum divinarum modos, etiam de singulis dici quod omnium est, propter inseparabilem operationem uniut ejusdemque substantiæ. In quinto decimo vero libro de Trinitate (Cap.
passages.english: showing the inseparability of the persons, he says: "Hence, by what he said, 'For the Father himself loves you' (John 16:27), he certainly does not separate himself; but he makes it understood according to the things I recalled above and sufficiently suggested, that each person in the Trinity is often named in such a way that the others too are understood there. So, then, it was said, 'For the Father himself loves you,' so that consequently the Son and the Holy Spirit are also understood." Again, a little later (Chap. 12, before the middle), the same Saint Augustine says this: "For we have already shown that in this Trinity, through many modes of divine expression, what belongs to all is said even of each individually, because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance." And in the fifteenth book On the Trinity (Chap.
passages.notes: "Unde se ab eo" is awkward; perhaps "unde se ab eo" should read "unde se ab eo [Patre]": 'he does not separate himself from him'. Rendered loosely as 'by what he said'.

passages.original: Quid igitur voluerunt sibi mystica munera inter abjecta praesepia, nisi ut intelligamus in Christo differentiam divinitatis et carnis? Ut homo nascitur, ut Deus adoratur. Jacet in panni.. sed fulget in stellis. Cunce nascentem indicant, stellæ dominantem. Caro est quæ involvitur, divinitas cui ab angelis ministratur. lta nec dignitas naturalis majestatis amittitur, et assumptæ carnis veritas comprobatur. Haec omnia quæ superius posita sunt hac beatus Ambrosius conclusione (Ibidem) firmavit, dicens : Hæc est fides nostra. Sic se Deus agnosci voluit ab hominibus. Nempe beatus 245 Ambrosius superiorem disputationem hac definitione concludens (Cap, 4), ita ut hanc esse diceret fidem nostram, evidentissime docuit, ut sicut Deum hominemque dicimus, sic divinitatem et carnem nullatenus dicere dubitemus.
passages.english: What, then, did the mystical gifts beside the lowly manger mean, unless that we should understand in Christ the difference of divinity and flesh? As man he is born, as God he is adored. He lies in swaddling clothes, but shines in the stars. The cradle shows him being born, the stars [show him] ruling. It is the flesh that is wrapped, the divinity that is served by angels. Thus neither is the dignity of his natural majesty lost, and the reality of the flesh he assumed is proved. All these things set out above blessed Ambrose confirmed with this conclusion (Ibid.), saying: "This is our faith. Thus God willed to be known by men." Surely blessed Ambrose, concluding the preceding discussion with this definition (Chap. 4), so as to say that this is our faith, taught most clearly that just as we call [him] God and man, so we should in no way hesitate to speak of divinity and flesh.
passages.notes: "panni.." read as pannis; "Cunce" as Cunae. 245 is a page marker.

passages.original: Beatus quoque Augustinus in libro de Fide, Spe, et Caritate, quem nosti a muttis Enchiridton nuncupari, sic dicit (Cap. 34) : Quis enim hoc solum congruenti- In,. explicet verbis, quod Verbum caro factum est ut habitaret in nobis: ut credamus Dei Patris omnipotentis unicum Filium, natum de Spiritu sancto et Virgine Maria? Ita quippe Verbum caro factum est, a divinitate carne suscepta, non in carnem divinitate mulata. Ecce beatus Augustinus ,ostendit divinitatem susceptricem carnis, quam nihilominus susceptricem testatur et mortis. In libro enim de Præsentia Dei sic dicit : Per caput nostrum reconciliamur Deo, quia in illo est divinitus Unigeniti facta particeps mortalitalis v nostræ, ut et nos participes ejus immortalitatis essemus.
passages.english: Blessed Augustine too, in the book On Faith, Hope and Charity, which you know is called by many the Enchiridion, says this (Chap. 34): "For who could explain in fitting words this alone, that the Word was made flesh to dwell among us, so that we believe in the only Son of God the Father almighty, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary? For the Word was made flesh in this way: by flesh being taken up by the divinity, not by the divinity being changed into flesh." See, blessed Augustine shows the divinity as the receiver of flesh, and he testifies that it is nonetheless also the receiver of death. For in the book On the Presence of God he says: "Through our head we are reconciled to God, because in him the divinity of the Only-begotten was made a sharer in our mortality, so that we too might be sharers in his immortality."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (muttis, Enchiridton, mulata, divinitus = divinitas, mortalitalis; stray 'In,.' and 'v' omitted).

passages.original: Supernos 251 ergo effusum est de Spiritu sancto. At vero super Dominum Jesum, cum iti forma esset hominis, manebat Spiritus; sicut scriptum est: Supra quem videris Spiritum descendentem de coelo, et manentem super eum, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu sancto (Joan. I, 33). Circa nos ex affluenti commodo liberalitas largientis est, in illo totius mane in æternum Spiritus plenitudo. Nempe beatos Ambrosius evidenter atque indubitanter ostendit animæ Christi plenam totius divinitatis inesse notitiam, cum dicit, quia circa nos ex affluenti commodo liberalitas largientis est, in illo totius manet in æternum Spiritus plenitudo. Hoc autem ut diceret, illum sermonem beati Joannis attendit, quo ait, cum de ipso Filio loqueretur: Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum (Joan.
passages.english: So upon us [something] of the Holy Spirit has been poured out. But upon the Lord Jesus, when he was in the form of a man, the Spirit remained; as it is written: "He on whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, he it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit" (John 1:33). Toward us there is the generosity of the giver from overflowing bounty; in him the fullness of the whole Spirit remains for ever. Surely blessed Ambrose shows clearly and beyond doubt that full knowledge of the whole divinity is present in the soul of Christ, when he says that toward us there is the generosity of the giver from overflowing bounty, while in him the fullness of the whole Spirit remains for ever. To say this, he had in view that saying of blessed John in which he says, when speaking of the Son himself: "For God does not give the Spirit by measure" (John
passages.notes: "mane" read as manet; 251 is a page marker. Reference completes in the following context (3:34).

passages.original: Quod beatus quoque Augustinus tadem sancti Spiritus illuminatione percipiens atque intelligens, in sola persona Christi accipi debere confirmat. Nam cum eumdem locum Evangelii explanasset (Tract. 14 in Joan.), ipso sermone Joannis Baptistæ proposito quo ait: Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum, idem beatus Augustinus ita subjecit: Quid est hoc : Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus I Spiritum? Invenimus, quia ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum ? Audi Apostolum dicentem: Secundum mensuram donationis Christi (Ephes. IV, 7). Hominibus ad mensuram dat, unico Filio non dat ad mensuram. Item in eadem homilia dicit : « Sic sunt etiam diversa dona fidelium, tanquam membris ad mensuram cuique propriam distributa. Sed Christus qui dat, non ad mensuram accepit. Audi enim adhuc quod sequitur, quia de Filio dixerat : Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum; Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus (Joan. III, 54). » Nempe beatus Augustinus ostendit hoc evangelico testimonio quid debeamus de anima Christi sentire, quando ipse Christus qui Spiritum dat, non ad mensuram accipit. Ipse est enim qui dat, ipse est qui accipit; et quia potens est ad mensuram dare, ideo non potuit ad mensuram accipere.
passages.english: Blessed Augustine too, perceiving and understanding this by the same illumination of the Holy Spirit, confirms that it must be taken of the person of Christ alone. For when he expounded the same passage of the Gospel (Tractate 14 on John), having set out the very saying of John the Baptist in which he says, "For God does not give the Spirit by measure," the same blessed Augustine added: "What is this: 'For God does not give the Spirit by measure'? Do we find that God gives the Spirit by measure? Hear the Apostle saying: 'According to the measure of the gift of Christ' (Eph. 4:7). To men he gives by measure; to the only Son he does not give by measure." Again in the same homily he says: "So too the gifts of the faithful are diverse, as if distributed to members, to each by its own measure. But Christ who gives did not receive by measure. For hear further what follows, since he had said of the Son, 'For God does not give the Spirit by measure': 'The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand' (John 3:35)." Surely blessed Augustine shows by this Gospel testimony what we ought to think about the soul of Christ, since Christ himself, who gives the Spirit, does not receive by measure. For he is the one who gives, he is the one who receives; and because he is able to give by measure, therefore he could not receive by measure.
passages.notes: "tadem" read as eadem. The printed reference 'Joan. III, 54' is evidently an error for 3:35.

passages.original: Quod in primo libro Retractationum suarum ostendens, inter alia sic ait: < Alio loco quod interposui testimonium: Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum (Joan. in, 54), nondum intellexeram de Christo proprie verius accipi. Aliis quippe hominibus nisi ad mensuram daretur Spiritus, non duplum peteret Elisæus quam fuit in Elia (IV Reg. II, 9). » In his ergo dictis beati Augustini illud maxime attendamus, quod ait, aliis hominibus ad mensuram Spiritum dari. Quod utique ideo dixit, ut hoc se non de divinitate, sed de humanitate Christi sensisse monstraret, cui non ad mensuram dedit Deus spiritum, cum unicuique dari gratiam secundum 252 mensuram donationis Christi testetur ApostoIus.
passages.english: Showing this in the first book of his Retractations, he says among other things: "In another place, regarding the testimony I inserted, 'For God does not give the Spirit by measure' (John 3:34), I had not yet understood that it is more truly taken as properly of Christ. For if the Spirit were not given to other men by measure, Elisha would not have asked for double what was in Elijah (4 Kings 2:9)." In these words of blessed Augustine, then, let us attend above all to what he says, that the Spirit is given to other men by measure. He said this, of course, to show that he understood this not of the divinity but of the humanity of Christ, to which God gave the Spirit not by measure, since the Apostle testifies that grace is given to each one according to the measure of the gift of Christ.
passages.notes: Printed reference 'Joan. in, 54' corrected to 3:34. 252 is a page marker.

passages.original: Frat ergo aliquid intus saucium, et aliquid foris sanum : corporis oculos habebat sanos, cordis habebat saucios. Factus est ille homo ad corporis oculum, ut credens in eum qui videri corporaliter potuit, curareris ad eum ipsum videndum, quem spiritaliter videre non poteras. His verbis ostendit beatus Augustinus in spiritalibus rebus hoc esse capere quod videre, neque aliud esse videre quam intelligere, nec intelligere aliud esse quam nosse. Hinc est quod in librode Præsentia Dei (Epist ad Dardanum alias 57, nunc 187), cum soli Filio dat plenam divinitatis capacitatem, soli plenam divinitatis ostendit inesse notitiam.
passages.english: So there was something wounded within and something sound without: he had sound eyes of the body, but wounded eyes of the heart. That man was made [visible] to the eye of the body, so that, believing in him who could be seen bodily, you might be healed to see that very one whom you could not see spiritually. With these words blessed Augustine shows that in spiritual matters to grasp is the same as to see, and to see is nothing other than to understand, and to understand nothing other than to know. Hence it is that in the book On the Presence of God (Letter to Dardanus, formerly 57, now 187), when he grants to the Son alone the full capacity for the divinity, he shows that full knowledge of the divinity is present in him alone.
passages.notes: "Frat" read as Erat. "Capacitas" here plays on capere ('grasp/contain').

passages.original: » Et cum idem beatus Augustinus a præceptis vitæ peragendæ illa præteriti temporis sacramenta discerneret, tanquam calicem dividens, postquam commemo. ravit quod dictum est: Non occides, non mæchaberis (Deut. v, 17, 18), et aliquanta quæ textu decalogi continentur, hæc ipse sanctus Augustinus subjecit, dicens : # Omnia ista ad vinum pertinent; illa vero carnalia quasi resederunt, ut remauereot apud illos, et effunderetur ideo omnis spiritalis intellectus. Calis enim in manu Domini, id est in potestate Domini;
passages.english: And when the same blessed Augustine was distinguishing those sacraments of past time from the precepts for conducting life, as if dividing the cup, after he had recalled what was said, "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery" (Deut. 5:17-18), and some other things contained in the text of the Decalogue, the same Saint Augustine added, saying: "All these pertain to the wine; but those carnal things settled as it were [to the bottom], so that they might remain with them, and so that all the spiritual understanding might be poured out. For the cup in the hand of the Lord, that is, in the power of the Lord;
passages.notes: "remauereot" read as remanerent, "Calis" as Calix. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: 18. Præ omnibus studium gerite libros sancti Augustini quos ad Prosperum et Hilarium scripsit, memoratis fratribus legendos ingerere. Quorum merrtionem beata? memoriae Hormisda, sedis apostolicæ gloriosus antistes, in epistola quam consulenti se sancto fratri consacerdotique nostro Possessori rescripsit, cum magno præconio catholice laudis inse, ruit.
passages.english: 18. Above all, make it your concern to press upon the brothers mentioned the reading of the books of Saint Augustine which he wrote to Prosper and Hilary. Hormisdas of blessed memory, glorious bishop of the apostolic see, inserted mention of these, with great proclamation of catholic praise, in the letter which he wrote in reply to our holy brother and fellow priest Possessor when he consulted him.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'merrtionem' = mentionem, 'beata?' = beatae, 'inse, ruit' = inseruit.

passages.original: Propterea etiam essentialem sive naturaleni factam naturarum unitionem omnimodis confitemur, non sicut illi qui tanquam in propheta, ita in Christo Deum Verbum h inoperasse contendunt. Quos cedar. guit beatus Gregorius Nazianzenus ad Clidoniom, dicens : < Si quis sicut in propheta secundum gratiam dicit inoperasse Deum Verbuli, et non essentialiter factam confitetur unitionem, sit vacuus melioris illoperatioris, magis autem plenus sit detorioris.
passages.english: For this reason we also confess in every way that the union of the natures was made essential or natural, not as those who contend that God the Word operated in Christ as in a prophet. These the blessed Gregory Nazianzen refuted, [writing] to Cledonius and saying: "If anyone says that God the Word operated [in him] by grace as in a prophet, and does not confess that the union was made essentially, let him be empty of the better operation, or rather let him be full of the worse.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'naturaleni' = naturalem, 'cedar. guit' = redarguit, 'Clidoniom' = Cledonium, 'Verbuli' = Verbum, 'illoperatioris' = inoperationis, 'detorioris' = deterioris; stray 'h' omitted. 'Inoperasse' renders Greek 'energein' (to operate/work in). The quotation continues into the following passage.

passages.original: Hoc autem non ejusdem carnis incorruptibilitas, sed resurrectionis celeritas fecit. His omnibus in quibus nostræ seminationis ac resurrectionis certissimam qualitatem verbis apostolicis sanctus Augustinus ostendit, dicens : Constat itaque, neque ullo modo dubitandum est, corpus Christi, quod licet corruptionem putredinis in sepulcro non senserit, quia scriptum est, < Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem (Psal. xv, 10), > clavis tamen et luncea corrumpi potut, nunc omnino in incorruptione persistere; et quod in contumelia passionis mortisque seminatum est, nune esse in gloria vitæ æternaæ;
passages.english: This, however, was brought about not by the incorruptibility of that same flesh, but by the swiftness of the resurrection. In all these [words], in which, through the apostle's words, Saint Augustine shows the most certain character of our sowing and resurrection, saying: "It is therefore established, and must in no way be doubted, that the body of Christ—which, although it did not experience the corruption of decay in the tomb, because it is written, 'You will not let your holy one see corruption' (Ps. 15:10), could nevertheless be corrupted by the nails and the lance—now abides entirely in incorruption; and that what was sown in the dishonour of suffering and death is now in the glory of eternal life;
passages.notes: The second sentence is syntactically incomplete ('His omnibus...' has no main verb before the quotation); possibly something has dropped out. Scanning errors corrected: 'luncea' = lancea, 'potut' = potuit, 'nune' = nunc. The quotation continues into the following passage.
